processing: A blend rather than a production style: pu-erh leaf, in today's shops usually ripe, is brewed or pressed together with dried chrysanthemum flowers.
harvest_season: No harvest of its own. The tea base follows ordinary pu-erh pickings and the flowers are a separate crop, so neither season is normally stated on the blend.
appearance_dry: Dark brown pu-erh leaf mixed with whole pale dried chrysanthemum heads, or a small dark tuo with flowers pressed in.
appearance_liquor: Deep reddish brown and clear, typical of ripe pu-erh, lifted slightly by the flowers.
appearance_wet: Soft dark leaf with swollen, pale flower heads among it.
taste_profile: Typical of the pairing: the smooth, earthy depth of ripe pu-erh with a light, fresh floral note and a gentle herbal sweetness from the chrysanthemum.

brewing.notes: Rinse quickly to wake the pu-erh. In a teapot for the table, a few flower heads to a normal dose of leaf is enough; too many and the blend turns medicinal. Adjust the ratio to taste.

vintage_note: Usually sold as an everyday blend, or simply mixed at the table, and seldom treated as a collectible vintage. Mini tuos may carry a production year, but the point is fresh-smelling flowers rather than age, so as with other flower blends it makes sense to buy recent stock. Any pu-erh you like can be turned into ju pu at home with a pinch of dried chrysanthemum.
description:
Ju pu is pu-erh with chrysanthemum, and it belongs to the tea houses of Hong Kong and Guangdong more than to any tea mountain. It is the most common flower pairing for pu-erh, the pot you may well be poured over dim sum.

There is no special processing behind it. Dried flowers, traditionally Hangzhou chrysanthemum, go into the pot with the leaf, or the two are pressed together into mini tuos. The flowers add a light fresh smell to a tea that can otherwise be heavy and cellar-like.

Expect the usual ripe pu-erh body, dark and soft, with a floral lift on top. Most of what goes wrong is proportion: a few flower heads are plenty. Brew it hot, rinse once, and keep the first steeps short, since a long steep of ripe tea can bury the flowers.

When buying, look at the flowers. Whole, clean heads with a clear smell beat dusty, broken ones. A mixed tuo is convenient, but buying the tea and the flowers separately lets you set the balance yourself and costs little.

Cantonese tradition credits the drink with clearing heat and helping digestion after a rich meal. Treat that as food lore, and as a good reason to order it with something fried.
history:
Little is documented about when ju pu first appeared. It is recorded as a tea-house drink of Hong Kong and Guangdong, known in Cantonese as guk pou or guk bou, where pu-erh is a standard companion to dim sum and adding flowers or pomelo rind to the pot is an ordinary habit.

Packed versions, loose or as small pressed tuos, now sell well beyond that region, including in Russian-speaking shops, but no maker or date of origin is on record.
